q: The cost of a fresh issue of equity shares works out higher than the cost of retained earnings of the same enterprise, mainly because:

options.A: New shares must be issued only at a premium fixed by law
options.B: Retained earnings also carry flotation costs at the same rate
options.C: Dividends on new shares are payable at a higher rate than on old shares
options.D: A fresh issue involves flotation costs such as underwriting and issue expenses, so the net amount realised per share is less than the issue price

e: Fresh equity bears flotation costs like underwriting and issue expenses, so net proceeds per share are less and its cost exceeds retained earnings.

q: Over-capitalisation of an enterprise is indicated when:

options.A: Its capital is insufficient to carry on its business efficiently
options.B: It has raised no debt capital at all
options.C: Its earnings are insufficient to give a fair return on the total capital employed, so that the real value of its shares falls below their book (par) value
options.D: Its current ratio is higher than that of similar enterprises

e: Over-capitalisation exists when earnings cannot give a fair return on capital employed, so real value of shares falls below book or par value.

q: A company issues 10% debentures of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 92 per debenture, redeemable at par after 10 years. Ignoring tax, the approximate cost of this debt, computed as the annual interest plus the annualised discount on redemption, divided by the average of the redemption value and the net proceeds, is:

A project is expected to yield annual sales of Rs 9,00,000 and annual cash operating costs of Rs 5,40,000. Depreciation on the project assets is Rs 60,000 per year and the tax rate is 30%. The annual cash flow after tax from the project is:
e: Profit = Rs 9,00,000 - Rs 5,40,000 - Rs 60,000 = Rs 3,00,000; after 30% tax Rs 2,10,000; add back depreciation Rs 60,000 gives Rs 2,70,000.

q: A project plant is depreciated by Rs 80,000 a year for 5 years and the tax rate is 25%. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 5 years at 12% is 3.605. The present value of the depreciation tax shield of the project is:
e: Annual tax shield = Rs 80,000 x 25% = Rs 20,000; present value = Rs 20,000 x 3.605 = Rs 72,100.

q: A machine costs Rs 6,00,000, has a life of 4 years with no salvage value and is depreciated on the straight-line basis. It is expected to give cash earnings (before depreciation and tax) of Rs 2,60,000 a year. The tax rate is 30% and the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 10% is 3.170. The Net Present Value of the machine is:
While computing the cash flows of a project for Net Present Value appraisal, the interest payable on the funds borrowed for the project is not deducted as a separate cash outflow, because:

options.A: Interest is never an expense of an enterprise
options.B: The financing cost is already taken into account through the discount rate applied to the cash flows, and deducting interest as well would count it twice
options.C: The project is always financed wholly out of equity
options.D: Interest is fully recovered out of the salvage value of the project

e: Financing cost is already reflected in the discount rate, so deducting interest again as a cash outflow would double-count it in NPV appraisal.

q: The present value of all the costs (capital and running) of a machine over its whole life is Rs 12,68,000. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the cost of capital is 3.170. The equivalent annual cost of the machine is:
e: Equivalent annual cost = present value of all costs / annuity factor = Rs 12,68,000 / 3.170 = Rs 4,00,000 per year.

q: A project has a Net Present Value of Rs 2,28,000 and the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the cost of capital is 3.800. Its equivalent annual annuity (equivalent annual benefit) is:
e: Equivalent annual annuity = NPV / annuity factor = Rs 2,28,000 / 3.800 = Rs 60,000 per year.

q: The equivalent annual cost method of comparing machines rests on the assumption that:

options.A: Each machine will be scrapped at the end of its life and never replaced
options.B: All the machines compared have exactly the same life
options.C: On the expiry of its life, a machine can be replaced by an identical machine on the same cost terms, so that the service is continued indefinitely
options.D: The running costs of a machine remain the same in every year of its life

e: The method assumes each machine can be replaced by an identical one on same terms at end of life, continuing the service indefinitely.

q: A new machine costs Rs 8,40,000. The old machine it replaces can be sold at once for Rs 1,20,000, and the replacement requires additional working capital of Rs 60,000 at the start. The net initial cash outlay on the replacement is:
e: Net initial outlay = new cost Rs 8,40,000 - sale of old Rs 1,20,000 + extra working capital Rs 60,000 = Rs 7,80,000.

q: A replacement is expected to save cash running expenses of Rs 3,20,000 a year before tax. It will carry additional depreciation of Rs 80,000 a year and the tax rate is 25%. The incremental annual cash inflow after tax from the replacement is:
e: Taxable saving = Rs 3,20,000 - Rs 80,000 = Rs 2,40,000; after 25% tax Rs 1,80,000; add back depreciation Rs 80,000 gives Rs 2,60,000.

q: The net initial outlay on a machine replacement is Rs 4,50,000. The replacement will give an incremental cash inflow after tax of Rs 1,30,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years, for which the cumulative present value (annuity) factor at the cost of capital is 3.791. The Net Present Value of the replacement is:

Funds of Rs 12,00,000 are available and the competing projects are divisible. Project Z requires Rs 5,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 2,00,000, Project X requires Rs 8,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 2,40,000 and Project Y requires Rs 6,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 1,20,000. Ranked by Profitability Index, Z is taken in full and the balance of the funds is invested in a part of X. The total Net Present Value of the combination so selected is:
e: By Profitability Index Z ranks first; Rs 5,00,000 in Z gives Rs 2,00,000 and Rs 7,00,000 part of X gives Rs 2,10,000, total NPV Rs 4,10,000.

q: Funds available are Rs 20,00,000 and the projects are indivisible. Project A requires Rs 12,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 3,60,000, Project B requires Rs 9,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 3,00,000, Project C requires Rs 11,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 3,30,000 and Project D requires Rs 8,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 2,20,000. The combination that maximises the total Net Present Value within the funds available is:

options.A: Projects B and C, giving a total Net Present Value of Rs 6,30,000
options.B: Projects A and D, giving a total Net Present Value of Rs 5,80,000
options.C: Projects C and D, giving a total Net Present Value of Rs 5,50,000
options.D: Project A alone, giving a Net Present Value of Rs 3,60,000

e: B plus C costs Rs 20,00,000 exactly and gives NPV Rs 3,00,000 + Rs 3,30,000 = Rs 6,30,000, higher than any other feasible combination.

q: Where funds are limited, the governing aim in selecting projects is to:

options.A: Choose the combination of projects which gives the highest total Net Present Value obtainable within the funds limit
options.B: Accept the single project having the highest internal rate of return
options.C: Accept the project having the largest initial outlay
options.D: Spread the funds equally over all the projects under consideration

e: With limited funds the aim is to select the combination of projects giving the highest total NPV obtainable within the funds limit.

q: At the end of a project's life, its plant is sold for Rs 1,50,000 when its written down (book) value is Rs 90,000. The gain on the sale is taxed at 30%. The after-tax salvage value to be taken as a cash inflow of the project is:

In the final year of a project, the operating cash inflow after tax is Rs 1,85,000, the after-tax salvage value of the plant is Rs 95,000 and working capital of Rs 60,000 invested at the start is recovered in full. The total cash inflow of the final year is:
e: Final year inflow = operating Rs 1,85,000 + salvage Rs 95,000 + working capital recovered Rs 60,000 = Rs 3,40,000.

q: The working capital invested in a project and recovered at the end of its life is not subjected to tax on its recovery, because:

options.A: Working capital is always provided out of tax-free funds
options.B: The recovery is a return of the amount invested and not an income or gain of the project
options.C: Working capital is recovered only in the form of stock in hand
options.D: The tax laws exempt all receipts of the final year of a project

e: Recovery of working capital is merely return of the amount invested, not income or gain, so it is not taxed on recovery.

q: A project's cash flows have been estimated in nominal (money) terms, that is, after allowing for the expected rise in prices. For consistency, these cash flows should be discounted at:

options.A: The real rate of discount, from which the effect of inflation has been removed
options.B: The risk-free rate of return only
options.C: The nominal rate of discount, which itself includes an allowance for inflation
options.D: The rate of depreciation charged on the project assets

e: Nominal cash flows allowing for inflation must be discounted at the nominal rate, which itself includes inflation, for consistency.

q: A project costs Rs 9,20,000 and is expected to give a uniform cash inflow after tax at the end of each year of its life. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the cost of capital is 4.000. The minimum annual cash inflow after tax at which the project just breaks even in Net Present Value terms (Net Present Value equal to zero) is:
e: Break-even annual inflow = initial cost / annuity factor = Rs 9,20,000 / 4.000 = Rs 2,30,000, at which NPV is zero.

q: The crossover (Fisher) rate in capital budgeting is the rate of discount at which:

options.A: The Net Present Value of a single project is exactly zero
options.B: The Net Present Values of two competing projects are equal, so that their ranking by Net Present Value reverses on either side of that rate
options.C: The internal rate of return of a project equals the inflation rate
options.D: The payback period of two projects becomes equal

e: The crossover or Fisher rate is where NPVs of two competing projects are equal, so their NPV ranking reverses on either side of it.

q: Two machines render identical service and output, but have different lives and different cost patterns. The machine to be preferred is the one which has:

options.A: The lower equivalent annual cost, since the comparison is thereby reduced to a common per-year basis despite the difference in lives
options.B: The higher initial capital cost, since it is likely to last longer
options.C: The lower total of undiscounted costs over its whole life
options.D: The shorter life, since it can be replaced sooner

e: For identical service with different lives, the lower equivalent annual cost is preferred as it compares machines on a common per-year basis.

q: Compared with a project whose cash inflows arise in the early years, a project whose inflows arise mainly in the distant future will, other things being equal, show:

options.A: No change in Net Present Value when the discount rate changes
options.B: A greater change in Net Present Value for a given change in the discount rate, because distant inflows are discounted more heavily
options.C: A higher Net Present Value at every discount rate
options.D: An internal rate of return unaffected by the timing of its inflows

e: Distant inflows are discounted more heavily, so their NPV changes more for a given change in discount rate than early inflows.

q: Judged by their market values, an enterprise has debt of Rs 18,00,000 with an after-tax cost of 7% and equity of Rs 42,00,000 with a cost of 13%. Its weighted average cost of capital is:
What chiefly distinguishes an investment centre from a profit centre is that the manager of an investment centre also:

options.A: Prepares the cash budget of the centre
options.B: Takes decisions on the capital assets to be acquired, retained or replaced in the centre, and is judged on the return earned on those assets
options.C: Fixes the wages of the staff working in the centre
options.D: Maintains the stores ledger of the centre

e: An investment centre manager also decides on capital assets to acquire, retain or replace and is judged on return on those assets, unlike a profit centre.

q: The performance of a pure cost centre is judged most appropriately by:

options.A: The profit earned by the centre during the period
options.B: The revenue generated by the centre during the period
options.C: How efficiently it has controlled its costs for the level of output or service actually rendered, as shown by cost variances and cost per unit
options.D: The return on the capital employed in the centre

e: A pure cost centre is judged on efficient cost control for output or service actually rendered, shown by cost variances and cost per unit.

q: The manager of a revenue centre is NOT ordinarily held accountable for:

options.A: The sales revenue earned by the centre
options.B: The sales volume achieved in the centre's territory
options.C: The selling and promotional expenses of the centre
options.D: The production cost of the goods sold by the centre

e: A revenue centre manager is accountable for revenue, volume and selling expenses, but not for production cost of goods sold, which he does not control.

q: A unit of an enterprise can properly be treated as a profit centre only when:

options.A: Its manager can significantly influence both the revenues earned by the unit and the costs incurred by it
options.B: The unit employs more than a prescribed number of staff
options.C: The unit sells its output only to outside customers
options.D: The unit maintains a separate bank account of its own

e: A unit is a profit centre only when its manager can significantly influence both its revenues and its costs.

q: A Divisional Railway Hospital renders treatment to railway beneficiaries without charging them for the services. For the purposes of responsibility accounting, such a hospital is best treated as a:

options.A: Profit centre, because its services have a value
options.B: Cost centre, to be judged on the cost and quality of the services it renders within its budget
options.C: Investment centre, because it uses costly medical equipment
options.D: Revenue centre, because it serves a large number of patients

e: A railway hospital giving free treatment earns no revenue, so it is a cost centre judged on cost and quality of service within budget.

q: Among the usual responsibility centres, the widest measure of decision-making autonomy is enjoyed by the manager of:

options.A: A cost centre
options.B: A revenue centre
options.C: A service centre
options.D: An investment centre

e: An investment centre manager has the widest autonomy, controlling revenues, costs and capital investment decisions of the centre.

q: For responsibility accounting to work, the system of cost and revenue collection must be so arranged that:

options.A: Every item of cost and revenue is identified with a definite responsibility centre and the manager answerable for it
options.B: All costs are first collected for the enterprise as a whole and apportioned at the year end
options.C: Only the cash transactions of each centre are recorded
options.D: The accounts of all centres are merged into a single profit and loss account

e: Responsibility accounting requires every cost and revenue item to be identified with a definite centre and the manager answerable for it.

q: A division shows a loss after the common head-office costs have been apportioned to it, but its own segment margin is positive. The sound conclusion for a decision on closing the division is that:

options.A: The division should be closed at once, since it shows a loss
options.B: The apportioned loss alone proves that the division is unprofitable in every sense
options.C: The division is contributing something towards meeting the common costs and the profit of the enterprise, so its closure cannot be justified on the post-apportionment loss alone
options.D: The common costs will disappear entirely if the division is closed

e: A positive segment margin means the division contributes towards common costs, so closure cannot be justified merely by loss after apportionment.

q: In judging the performance of the manager of a profit centre, the figure on which attention is centred is the centre's:

options.A: Gross sales for the period
options.B: Controllable profit, that is, the revenues of the centre less the costs that are under the manager's control
options.C: Net profit after charging every cost of the enterprise
options.D: Capital employed at the close of the period

e: A profit centre manager is judged on controllable profit: centre revenues minus costs under his control, not profit after all enterprise costs.

q: Which of the following costs of a production shop is ordinarily controllable by the shop manager himself?

options.A: The wages of the workers engaged and supervised by him in the shop
options.B: The rent of the factory building fixed by a lease signed by the head office
options.C: The depreciation of plant purchased under a head-office decision
options.D: The head-office administration expenses apportioned to the shop

e: Wages of workers engaged and supervised by the shop manager are ordinarily controllable by him, unlike lease rent, depreciation or head-office costs.

q: For the manager of a workshop shop, which of the following is an uncontrollable cost?

options.A: The cost of consumable stores drawn for the jobs in his shop
options.B: The overtime wages authorised by him for work in his shop
options.C: The power charges for the machines operated in his shop, where he can regulate their running
options.D: The share of the central canteen subsidy and head-office expenses apportioned to his shop by the accounts office

e: Apportioned central canteen subsidy and head-office expenses are decided elsewhere and are uncontrollable for the workshop shop manager.

q: The depreciation charged on a machine in a section is uncontrollable by the section foreman mainly because:

options.A: Depreciation is not a real cost at all
options.B: The foreman does not maintain the fixed asset register
options.C: The machine was selected and purchased under a decision taken at a higher level, and the charge follows from that past decision rather than from anything the foreman now does
options.D: Depreciation is always charged to the head office account

e: Depreciation follows a past higher-level purchase decision on the machine, not anything the foreman now does, so it is uncontrollable by him.

q: If managers are regularly judged on costs which they have no power to influence, the most likely result is that:

options.A: Cost control in the enterprise improves automatically
options.B: The managers lose faith in the fairness of the reporting system and are demotivated, and may take distorted decisions to protect their reported results
options.C: The uncontrollable costs themselves begin to fall
options.D: The need for budgets disappears altogether

e: Judging managers on uncontrollable costs makes reporting seem unfair, demotivates them and may distort decisions taken to protect reported results.

q: Consider the following statements: 1. Every variable cost is controllable by the manager of the centre in which it is incurred. 2. Every fixed cost is uncontrollable by that manager. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Controllability depends on level and time, not cost behaviour alone; some variable costs are uncontrollable and some fixed costs controllable, so neither statement holds.

q: Inter-divisional transfers are recorded at a transfer price mainly so that:

options.A: The total profit of the enterprise as a whole is increased
options.B: Tax is saved on the internal movements of goods
options.C: The profit of the supplying division and the profit of the receiving division can each be measured, the transfer price dividing the enterprise's profit between them without by itself changing that total profit
options.D: The goods transferred cease to form part of the stock of the enterprise

e: Transfer pricing lets supplying and receiving divisions each measure their profit; it divides total profit between them without changing that total.

q: The general rule for the minimum transfer price that a supplying division should be willing to accept is that it should be at least equal to:

options.A: The incremental (variable) cost per unit of the goods transferred plus any opportunity cost per unit arising from the transfer
options.B: The full absorption cost per unit plus the normal profit margin of the enterprise
options.C: The highest price charged to any outside customer
options.D: The budgeted cost of the receiving division per unit

e: Minimum transfer price = incremental variable cost per unit plus opportunity cost per unit lost by transferring internally.

q: A supplying division produces a part at a variable cost of Rs 55 per unit and has spare capacity which has no other use. The lowest transfer price it should accept for supplying the part to another division is:

options.A: Rs 70 per unit
options.B: Rs 55 per unit
options.C: Nil
options.D: Rs 40 per unit

e: With spare capacity opportunity cost is nil, so lowest acceptable price is just variable cost, Rs 55 per unit.

q: A supplying division works at full capacity. Its variable cost is Rs 70 per unit and, for every unit transferred internally, it gives up a contribution of Rs 30 per unit that it could have earned on outside sales. The lowest transfer price it should accept is:

options.A: Rs 70 per unit
options.B: Rs 40 per unit
options.C: Rs 30 per unit
options.D: Rs 100 per unit

e: At full capacity minimum price = variable cost Rs 70 + lost contribution Rs 30 = Rs 100 per unit.

q: The open market price of an article transferred between divisions is Rs 260 per unit. On an internal transfer, the supplying division saves Rs 15 per unit of packing, selling and delivery expenses that an outside sale would have required. A fair market-based transfer price is:

options.A: Rs 245 per unit
options.B: Rs 275 per unit
options.C: Rs 260 per unit
options.D: Rs 230 per unit

e: Market-based price = open market Rs 260 - saving on internal transfer Rs 15 = Rs 245 per unit.

q: A supplying division incurs a total cost of Rs 85 per unit on an article. Transfers are priced on the cost-plus basis with a mark-up of 20 per cent on cost. The transfer price per unit is:

options.A: Rs 85
options.B: Rs 105
options.C: Rs 102
options.D: Rs 68

e: Cost-plus transfer price = Rs 85 x (1 + 20%) = Rs 85 + Rs 17 = Rs 102 per unit.

q: Where transfers are priced at standard cost instead of at the actual cost incurred by the supplying division:

options.A: The receiving division bears all the inefficiencies of the supplying division
options.B: The supplying division itself bears its cost variances, so its inefficiencies are not passed on to the receiving division
options.C: No profit can be computed for either division
options.D: The transfer price changes with every change in the actual cost

e: At standard cost, the supplying division bears its own variances, so its inefficiencies are not passed on to the receiving division.

q: Pricing inter-divisional transfers at marginal (variable) cost alone suffers from the drawback that the supplying division:

options.A: Recovers none of its fixed costs and shows no profit on the transfers, which weakens both its reported performance and its motivation
options.B: Is forced to sell the same article to outsiders at the same price
options.C: Has to pay a share of its profit to the receiving division
options.D: Cannot ascertain the variable cost of the article

e: Marginal-cost pricing lets the supplying division recover no fixed costs and show no profit on transfers, weakening performance and motivation.

q: A recognised drawback of the dual-pricing method of transfer pricing is that:

options.A: Only one division is allowed to record the transfer
options.B: The supplying division is never credited for the transfer
options.C: The receiving division is charged at the market price in every case
options.D: The profits reported by the divisions, when added together, exceed the profit of the enterprise as a whole, and a reconciliation adjustment becomes necessary

e: In dual pricing divisions use different prices, so summed divisional profits exceed enterprise profit and a reconciliation adjustment is needed.

q: The transfer price of an article is fixed well above the price at which the receiving division can buy the same article in the open market, although the supplying division has idle capacity. The likely outcome, harmful to the enterprise as a whole, is that the receiving division will:

options.A: Increase its purchases from the supplying division
options.B: Stop producing the final product altogether
options.C: Buy the article from outside suppliers, leaving the supplying division's idle capacity unused
options.D: Reduce the selling price of the final product

e: If transfer price exceeds outside market price despite idle capacity, the receiving division will buy outside, leaving internal capacity unused and harming the firm.

q: A division earns the same profit as before but the capital employed in it is reduced by disposing of idle assets. Its Return on Investment will:

options.A: Fall, because the assets have been reduced
options.B: Rise, because the same profit is now earned on a smaller capital base
options.C: Remain exactly unchanged
options.D: Become equal to its residual income

e: ROI = profit / capital employed; same profit on a smaller capital base after disposing idle assets gives a higher return on investment.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 3,60,000 on a capital employed of Rs 24,00,000. Its Return on Investment is:
Residual Income of a division is arrived at by deducting, from the profit of the division:

options.A: A capital charge worked out by applying the required rate of return (cost of capital) to the capital employed in the division
options.B: The depreciation charged on the assets of the division
options.C: The dividend declared by the enterprise for the year
options.D: The fixed costs of the division for the period

e: Residual Income = divisional profit minus a capital charge, being required rate of return applied to capital employed in the division.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 4,20,000 on a capital employed of Rs 28,00,000. The required rate of return is 11 per cent. The Residual Income of the division is:
A division earns a profit of Rs 2,40,000 on a capital employed of Rs 30,00,000, on which the required rate of return is 10 per cent. Its Residual Income is:

options.D: Nil

q: A division at present earns a Return on Investment of 18 per cent, while the cost of capital of the enterprise is 12 per cent. A new proposal before it would earn 14 per cent on the additional capital required. Judged strictly by Return on Investment, the divisional manager is likely to reject the proposal, although:

options.A: Accepting it would increase the Residual Income of the division, since 14 per cent exceeds the 12 per cent cost of capital
options.B: The proposal would reduce the total profit of the enterprise
options.C: The proposal earns less than the cost of capital
options.D: Residual Income would also fall if the proposal were accepted

e: The proposal earns 14%, above the 12% cost of capital, so it would raise Residual Income even though an ROI-focused manager may reject it.

q: A limitation of comparing divisions of very different sizes by Residual Income alone is that:

options.A: Residual Income cannot be computed for a large division
options.B: Residual Income takes no account of the capital employed
options.C: Being an absolute money amount, it tends to be larger for a bigger division simply because of its size, so the comparison may mislead
options.D: Residual Income is always negative for a small division

e: Residual Income is an absolute money amount, so bigger divisions naturally show larger amounts and size alone can mislead comparisons.

q: The capital charge deducted in computing Residual Income represents, in substance:

options.A: The tax payable on the profit of the division
options.B: The dividend expected by the shareholders of the enterprise
options.C: The depreciation of the assets employed in the division
options.D: The opportunity cost of the funds locked up in the division, that is, the return those funds could have earned in their next best use

e: The capital charge is the opportunity cost of funds locked in the division, the return those funds could earn in their next best use.

q: The Net Operating Profit After Tax of an enterprise is Rs 7,50,000, its capital employed is Rs 50,00,000 and its weighted average cost of capital is 9 per cent. Its Economic Value Added is:

An enterprise reports a Net Operating Profit After Tax of Rs 6,00,000 on a capital employed of Rs 80,00,000. Its weighted average cost of capital is 10 per cent. The correct reading of its Economic Value Added of (-) Rs 2,00,000 is that:

options.A: Despite showing an accounting profit, the enterprise has earned less than its cost of capital and has therefore destroyed value during the period
options.B: The enterprise has necessarily incurred a cash loss during the period
options.C: The cost of capital has been computed wrongly in every such case
options.D: The enterprise should stop preparing its profit and loss account

e: EVA of (-) Rs 2,00,000 means operating profit covered less than the cost of capital, so value was destroyed despite an accounting profit.

q: Which of the following actions will, other things remaining equal, increase the Economic Value Added of an enterprise?

options.A: Investing fresh capital in a project expected to earn less than the cost of capital
options.B: Allowing idle assets to remain locked up in low-yielding activities
options.C: Shifting capital out of activities earning below the cost of capital into activities earning above it
options.D: Increasing the capital employed without any increase in operating profit

e: Shifting capital from activities earning below cost of capital to those earning above it raises EVA, other things equal.

q: The Economic Value Added of an enterprise for a year works out to exactly zero. This means that:

options.A: The enterprise has made neither a profit nor a loss in its books
options.B: Its operating profit after tax has just covered the full cost of the capital employed, so the investors have received exactly the return they required and no excess value has been created
options.C: The enterprise employs no borrowed capital at all
options.D: Its Residual Income must necessarily be negative

e: EVA zero means NOPAT just covered the full cost of capital employed, giving investors exactly their required return with no excess value created.

q: Under the Balanced Scorecard, the objectives set under each of its perspectives are given practical shape through a set of:

options.A: Ledger accounts and subsidiary registers
options.B: Audit objections and their replies
options.C: Sanction orders issued by the competent authority
options.D: Measures, targets and initiatives — the measure to be watched, the level to be reached and the action programmes for reaching it

e: Under each Balanced Scorecard perspective, objectives are made practical through measures, targets and initiatives to reach those targets.

q: In the cause-and-effect chain underlying the Balanced Scorecard, improvements are expected to flow in the order:

options.A: Learning and growth, leading to better internal processes, leading to better customer outcomes, leading finally to better financial results
options.B: Financial results, leading to customer outcomes, leading to internal processes, leading to learning and growth
options.C: Customer outcomes, leading to learning and growth, leading to financial results, leading to internal processes
options.D: Internal processes, leading to learning and growth, leading to financial results, leading to customer outcomes

e: The chain runs learning and growth to better internal processes, to better customer outcomes, and finally to better financial results.

q: A practical difficulty in working the Balanced Scorecard is that:

options.A: It provides no financial measure of any kind
options.B: It cannot be applied outside a manufacturing concern
options.C: Its success rests on identifying the right measures and the true cause-and-effect links between them; badly chosen measures can direct effort in the wrong direction
options.D: It requires the annual accounts to be abandoned

e: The Scorecard depends on choosing right measures and true cause-and-effect links; badly chosen measures can direct effort wrongly.

q: For a railway division applying the Balanced Scorecard, which of the following measures fits the customer perspective most appropriately?

options.A: The cost per train kilometre worked out for the division
options.B: The percentage of passenger complaints redressed within the prescribed time and the level of passenger satisfaction with the services
options.C: The number of staff who completed a training course during the year
options.D: The percentage of defective components turned out by the workshops

e: Passenger complaints redressed within time and passenger satisfaction are customer perspective measures for a railway division.

q: When the Balanced Scorecard is applied to a government undertaking such as a zonal railway, its financial perspective is suitably recast to lay stress on:

options.A: Maximising the market price of the undertaking's shares
options.B: Declaring the highest possible dividend every year
options.C: Dispensing with financial targets altogether
options.D: Meeting the financial targets set for it, such as earning a surplus over working expenses, recovering costs and keeping expenditure within the budgetary allotments

e: For a government undertaking like a railway, the financial perspective stresses meeting set targets: surplus over working expenses, cost recovery and budget limits.

q: As performance reports pass from the operating level to successively higher levels of management, sound practice is that they become:

options.A: Increasingly summarised and aggregated, the greatest detail being given at the operating level where corrective action is actually taken
options.B: Increasingly detailed, so that the top management sees every transaction
options.C: Identical in form and content at every level
options.D: Less frequent at the operating level than at the top level

e: Reports become increasingly summarised as they go up, with greatest detail at the operating level where corrective action is taken.

q: A responsibility performance report serves its purpose of control mainly because it sets out, for the centre concerned:

options.A: Only the actual figures for the month, without any standard for comparison
options.B: The figures of every other centre in the enterprise
options.C: The budgeted figures, the actual results and the variances between them, so that the manager and his superiors can see where action is called for
options.D: The audited figures of the previous financial year

e: A responsibility report shows budget, actuals and variances for the centre, so the manager and superiors can see where action is needed.

q: A performance report which reaches the manager long after the period to which it relates loses most of its control value, because:

options.A: The figures in it cease to be accurate after the period ends
options.B: Corrective action taken on its basis can no longer affect the results of that period, which have already been incurred
options.C: Delayed reports are not accepted by the statutory auditors
options.D: The budget for the period is automatically cancelled

e: A late report has little control value because corrective action can no longer affect results of the period already incurred.

q: For a fuller picture of the performance of a railway division, its periodic performance review properly brings in, along with the financial results, operating and service indicators such as:

options.A: Only the balances standing in the suspense accounts of the division
options.B: Only the leave balances of the staff of the division
options.C: Only the earnings of the other divisions of the zone
options.D: Safety performance, punctuality of train services and failures of assets in service

e: Divisional review should add operating indicators like safety, punctuality and asset failures to financial results for a fuller picture.

q: Job costing is most suitably applied where:

options.A: A single homogeneous product is manufactured continuously in bulk
options.B: Work is undertaken against a specific order of a customer and each order remains separately identifiable throughout production
options.C: Services are rendered to the public at large, as in a transport undertaking
options.D: A liquid is passed through a series of continuous processes

e: Job costing suits work done against a specific customer order, each order remaining separately identifiable throughout production.

q: Under job costing, the profit or loss on a job is ordinarily ascertained:

options.A: At the end of every week, whether the job is complete or not
options.B: Only at the end of the financial year for all jobs together
options.C: Separately for each job, when that job is completed, by comparing its total cost with the price charged for it
options.D: By dividing the total profit of the factory equally among all the jobs executed

e: Profit or loss is found separately for each job on completion, by comparing its total cost with the price charged for that job.

q: A pharmaceutical concern manufactures medicines in definite lots, all the units in a lot being identical and produced together. The method of costing most appropriate for it is:

options.A: Batch costing, each lot being treated as a batch
options.B: Contract costing, each lot being treated as a contract
options.C: Operating costing, each lot being treated as a service
options.D: Process costing, each lot being treated as a separate process

e: Medicines made in definite identical lots suit batch costing, with each lot treated as a batch cost unit.

q: In process costing, normal loss means the loss of material which:

options.A: Arises only because of theft or pilferage in the process
options.B: Can always be avoided by careful handling of the material
options.C: Is valued and charged in full to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.D: Is inherent in the nature of the process and is expected to occur even under efficient working conditions

e: Normal loss is inherent in the process and expected even under efficient working conditions, unlike avoidable abnormal loss.

q: In a process, 5,600 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 1,40,000. Normal loss is 10% of the input and the scrap realises Rs 25 per unit. The cost per unit of good output is:
e: Good output = 5,600 - 560 = 5,040 units; net cost = Rs 1,40,000 - 560 x Rs 25 = Rs 1,26,000; cost per unit = Rs 1,26,000 / 5,040 = Rs 25.00.

q: A job which is still incomplete at the close of the accounting year is shown in the cost accounts as:

options.A: A loss of the year, since it has earned no revenue
options.B: Work-in-progress, at the cost accumulated on it up to that date
options.C: Finished stock, at its estimated selling price
options.D: A suspense item, at the price quoted to the customer

e: An incomplete job at year end is shown as work-in-progress at the cost accumulated on it up to that date.

q: In batch costing, the set-up cost incurred for a batch is spread over all the units in that batch. It follows that, other things remaining equal, the set-up cost per unit:

options.A: Rises as the size of the batch increases
options.B: Is the same whatever the size of the batch
options.C: Falls as the size of the batch increases, because the same set-up cost is shared by a larger number of units
options.D: Depends only on the selling price of the product

e: Set-up cost per unit = total set-up cost / batch size, so it falls as batch size increases, the same cost being shared by more units.

q: In process costing, abnormal loss means the loss which:

options.A: Is in excess of the normal loss expected in the process and arises from avoidable causes such as inefficiency, carelessness or an accident
options.B: Is inherent in the process and cannot be avoided under any circumstances
options.C: Has no scrap value under any circumstances
options.D: Is borne by the good output of the process as a part of its cost

e: Abnormal loss exceeds normal expected loss and arises from avoidable causes like inefficiency, carelessness or accident.

q: Where the output of one process becomes the input of the next process, the cost of the output transferred from the earlier process is treated in the account of the succeeding process as:

options.A: A selling and distribution expense of that process
options.B: An abnormal loss of that process
options.C: A credit balance carried forward to the next period
options.D: The cost of material consumed by that process, appearing as the first item of its cost

e: Output transferred from an earlier process becomes material input of the next process and appears as its first cost item.

q: In a factory following job costing, direct materials issued from the stores for a particular job are charged to that job on the basis of:

options.A: The purchase invoices received from the suppliers during the week
options.B: Material requisition notes which bear the number of the job for which the material is drawn
options.C: The monthly stores summary, divided equally among all the jobs in hand
options.D: The gate pass issued when the material first entered the stores

e: Direct materials are charged to a job from material requisition notes bearing that job number, identifying material drawn for it.

q: The total cost of a batch of 2,500 identical units is Rs 1,87,500. The cost per unit of the batch is:

options.A: Rs 60
options.B: Rs 75
options.C: Rs 85
options.D: Rs 125

e: Cost per unit = total batch cost / units = Rs 1,87,500 / 2,500 = Rs 75 per unit.

q: In process costing, each process is represented by a separate process account. This account is credited with:

options.A: The value of the output transferred to the next process or to finished stock, together with the scrap value of the normal loss and the value of any abnormal loss
options.B: Only the wages paid to the workers employed in the process
options.C: The selling price of the finished product of the factory as a whole
options.D: The capital cost of the plant installed in the process

e: A process account is credited with output transferred onward, scrap value of normal loss and value of any abnormal loss.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes job costing from batch costing?

options.A: Job costing is used for services, while batch costing is used only for goods
options.B: In job costing the cost unit is a group of identical articles, while in batch costing it is a single order
options.C: There is no difference at all between the two methods
options.D: In job costing the cost unit is one distinct job or order, while in batch costing the cost unit is a batch of identical articles produced together

e: In job costing the cost unit is one distinct job or order; in batch costing it is a batch of identical articles produced together.

q: In process costing, equivalent production has to be worked out mainly in order to:

options.A: Decide the selling price of the finished product
options.B: Value the work-in-progress and the completed output fairly, when some units are only partly complete at the end of the period
options.C: Compute the scrap value of the normal loss of the process
options.D: Apportion the joint costs among the joint products

e: Equivalent production values partly complete units fairly, so work-in-progress and completed output are costed correctly.

q: In a process, 5,500 units were completed and transferred to the next process during a period. The closing work-in-progress is 1,200 units, which are 75% complete in respect of all cost elements, and there was no opening work-in-progress. The equivalent production for the period is:

options.A: 6,700 units
options.B: 5,800 units
options.C: 6,100 units
options.D: 6,400 units

e: Equivalent production = 5,500 completed + 1,200 x 75% = 5,500 + 900 = 6,400 units.

q: Contract costing is also described as terminal costing because:

options.A: The cost of a contract is finally ascertained when the contract is completed and its account is terminated
options.B: Every contract must be completed within one accounting year
options.C: The contract account is closed every month without exception
options.D: It is applied only to work done at a railway terminal station

e: Contract costing is called terminal costing because cost is finally ascertained when the contract completes and its account is terminated.

q: In contract costing, notional profit means:

options.A: The cash received from the contractee minus the cash paid by the contractor
options.B: The difference between the value of work certified and the cost of the work so certified
options.C: The profit estimated to arise on the whole contract when it is completed
options.D: The retention money withheld by the contractee on the work certified

e: Notional profit = value of work certified minus cost of work so certified, on work done up to that date.

q: In contract costing, work certified means the work which:

options.A: Has been physically executed at the site but not yet measured by anyone
options.B: The contractor himself estimates to have been completed at the end of the year
options.C: Has been measured and approved by the engineer or architect of the contractee and forms the basis of payment to the contractor
options.D: Has been executed by the sub-contractors engaged on the contract

e: Work certified is work measured and approved by the contractee's engineer or architect and forms the basis of payment.

q: On an incomplete contract, the value of work certified is less than one-fourth of the contract price and a notional profit has arisen. The profit to be credited to the Profit and Loss Account is:

options.A: The whole of the notional profit
options.B: One-third of the notional profit, adjusted for cash received
options.C: Two-thirds of the notional profit, adjusted for cash received
options.D: Nil; the whole of the notional profit is carried forward as a reserve in the work-in-progress

e: If work certified is under one-fourth of contract price, no notional profit is credited to profit and loss; it is held as reserve in work-in-progress.

q: On a contract, the notional profit is Rs 90,000 and the value of work certified is 40% of the contract price. Cash received is 80% of the work certified. Using the rule applicable where work certified is between one-fourth and one-half of the contract price, the profit to be credited to the Profit and Loss Account is:
e: Profit credited = 1/3 x notional profit x cash ratio = 1/3 x Rs 90,000 x 80% = Rs 24,000.

q: Materials which remain unused at the contract site at the end of an accounting period are dealt with in the contract account by:

options.A: Charging their full cost to the contract of the year and writing them off as a loss
options.B: Crediting the contract account with their value, so that only the materials actually consumed are charged to the work of the period
options.C: Treating them as the personal property of the contractor
options.D: Adding their value to the value of work certified for the period

e: Unused materials at site are credited to the contract account, so only materials actually consumed are charged to the period's work.

q: The allowable cost of a cost-plus contract is Rs 6,40,000 and the contractor is entitled to a profit of 15% on cost. The contract price payable to the contractor is:
e: Contract price = cost + 15% profit = Rs 6,40,000 x 1.15 = Rs 7,36,000.

q: Where a contractor fails to complete a contract within the time agreed and the contract provides for liquidated damages for the delay, the amount so recovered is:

options.A: An additional profit of the contract to be shared with the contractor
options.B: Treated as a part of the value of work certified on the contract
options.C: A free income which has no connection with the contract account
options.D: Deducted from the amounts payable to the contractor under the contract, as compensation for the delay

e: Liquidated damages for delay are deducted from amounts payable to the contractor as compensation under the contract.

q: In job costing, comparing the actual cost of a completed job with the estimate or quotation prepared for it before its execution chiefly serves to:

options.A: Show whether the estimate was realistic and where the estimating or the execution of the job needs to improve
options.B: Fix the wages payable to the workers who worked on the job
options.C: Value the closing stock of materials in the stores
options.D: Decide the depreciation to be charged on the factory plant

e: Comparing actual job cost with its prior estimate shows whether estimating was realistic and where execution or estimating must improve.

q: In a process account, the scrap value realised from the normal loss of the process is:

options.A: Credited to the Costing Profit and Loss Account as an abnormal gain
options.B: Credited to the process account, so that the cost of the good output is reduced to that extent
options.C: Debited to the process account as an additional cost of the process
options.D: Ignored altogether in the cost accounts

e: Scrap value of normal loss is credited to the process account, reducing the cost borne by good output to that extent.

q: In some processes, a part of the material input disappears through evaporation or shrinkage and leaves nothing that can be sold. Such a loss:

options.A: Is valued at the selling price of the finished product
options.B: Is charged in full to the Costing Profit and Loss Account in every case
options.C: Has no realisable scrap value, and its cost is borne by the good output of the process
options.D: Must be recovered in cash from the workers handling the process

e: Loss by evaporation or shrinkage has no scrap value, so its cost is borne by the good output of the process.

q: In a railway workshop following job costing, costs are collected for repair and manufacturing work under the number of:

options.A: The pay bill of the workshop for the month
options.B: The work order opened for that specific work, to which the labour, material and on-cost expended on it are charged
options.C: The stores ledger folio of the material issued
options.D: The annual budget head of the workshop

e: In a railway workshop, costs are collected under the work order number opened for that specific repair or manufacturing work.

q: In contract costing, a separate contract account is opened in the contract ledger for:

options.A: All the contracts in hand taken together as one account
options.B: Each accounting year, covering every contract of that year
options.C: Each sub-contractor engaged by the contractor
options.D: Each contract, identified by its contract number, so that the cost and profit of that contract alone are ascertained

e: A separate contract account is opened for each contract by its number, so cost and profit of that contract alone are ascertained.

q: In a process, 9,600 units are introduced and the normal loss is 10% of the input. The actual output obtained is 8,750 units. The position is:

options.A: An abnormal loss of 850 units
options.B: An abnormal gain of 110 units
options.C: An abnormal loss of 110 units
options.D: Neither abnormal loss nor abnormal gain

e: Expected output = 9,600 - 10% = 8,640 units; actual 8,750 exceeds it by 110 units, so there is an abnormal gain of 110 units.

q: In a process, 7,200 units are introduced and the normal loss is 5% of the input. The actual output obtained is 6,700 units. The abnormal loss is:

options.A: 500 units
options.B: 360 units
options.C: 140 units
options.D: Nil

e: Expected output = 7,200 - 5% = 6,840 units; actual 6,700 is 140 units less, so abnormal loss = 140 units.
